query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing a portion of the Co in FeCoNi with Cr will induce local lattice distortions and magnetic inhomogeneities that impede domain wall motion, thereby increasing the coercivity of the resulting high‐entropy alloy relative to the pure FeCoNi and its Pd- or Pt-containing derivatives.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, single-phase fcc FeCoNi alloy known for its high saturation magnetization and low coercive field.
generation.intervention: Substitute approximately 25 at.% of Co with Cr (yielding an equiatomic FeCoNiCr alloy) while preserving a multicomponent, high-entropy (≥1.0R) almost equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Prepare the alloy by standard melting/casting and homogenization treatments designed to maintain a predominantly fcc (or controlled dual-phase) microstructure. The processing temperature and cooling rate should be chosen to ensure high configurational entropy and minimal phase segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Introduction of Cr atoms creates local lattice distortions and disruption in the uniform exchange interactions, thereby generating enhanced magnetic anisotropy and effective domain-wall pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: Cr, which has a different magnetic moment and tends toward antiferromagnetic coupling relative to Fe, Co, and Ni, will modify the local magnetic exchange interactions. This slight disruption increases the energy barrier for domain wall motion (i.e. raises effective anisotropy), resulting in higher coercivity without excessively sacrificing the high saturation magnetization of the base alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline FeCoNi, the FeCoNiCr alloy is expected to show a significantly increased coercive field under identical measurement conditions while still maintaining a high saturation magnetization. The exact magnitude of the coercivity increase is uncertain but should be measurably higher than that of the soft magnetic FeCoNi and its Pd/Pt derivatives.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic fcc FeCoNi alloy with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
generation.boundary: This outcome is anticipated when the processing conditions maintain a single-phase (or well-controlled dual-phase) high-entropy structure. Excessive phase decomposition or formation of unwanted secondary phases could negate the beneficial anisotropy effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise coercivity enhancement is not predetermined and may depend on details such as elemental distribution, degree of lattice strain, and microstructural homogeneity. Optimization of the Cr substitution level and processing parameters may be required for best performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set being the parent equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and the other set an equiatomic FeCoNiCr alloy (with ~25 at.% Cr replacing Co). Process both sample sets under identical melting, homogenization, and cooling conditions to ensure comparability of the microstructure. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops of both sets using vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) at room temperature and under identical applied field conditions.
measurements: Coercive field (Hc) from the hysteresis loops
Saturation magnetization (Ms) for magnetic performance comparison
Microstructural characterization (e.g., XRD, TEM) to confirm phase purity and grain size
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCoNiCr alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in the coercive field relative to the FeCoNi baseline (taking into account any measurement uncertainties) while maintaining a comparable high value of saturation magnetization, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 1A shows magnetization vs magnetic field (M-H) hysteresis loops measured at 300 K for heat-treated AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi. The loops suggest soft ferromagnetic properties. AlCoFeNi has a saturation magnetization (MS) of 99.8 Am2/kg and a coercivity (Hc) of 1.45 mT. When half of the Co is replaced by Cr in the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA, MS decreases to 46.2 Am2/kg, while Hc increases to 9.56 mT. The HEAs are almost fully magnetically saturated at fields of 500 mT. Figure 1B shows a comparison of MS and HC for AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEAs with other HEAs and benchmark soft magnetic materials (; ; ; ; ). The magnetic properties of the HEAs that we have studied are similar to others. The HEAs have higher values of HC than those of some soft magnetic materials (e.g., Permalloy, Hiperco). We do not claim that their soft magnetic properties are superior. Instead, we focus on the reasons for the substantial difference in magnetic properties when 50% Co is replaced by Cr in AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi.
